source_text: Possunt enim homines omne vitare peccatum, cum possunt vincere concupiscentiae malum. Si enim libido naturale malum est, et vincitur amore virtutis; multo magis - dicis - illa omnia vitia superari, quae de sola voluntate contingunt Si connivero - sicut dicis - invictum esse libidinis malum, profitebor me esse turpitudinis advocatum: si autem dixero, malum me quidem hoc naturale dixisse, sed quod vinci possit, id est, possit caveri
pass_a_gloss: Are-able for human-beings every vitare sin, when/with are-able vincere of-desire evil. if for lust natural evil is, and vincitur amore of-virtue; multo more - you-say - that all-things faults superari, which about/from alone by-will contingunt if connivero - as you-say - invictum to-be of-lust evil, profitebor me to-be of-shamefulness advocatum: if however dixero, evil me indeed this natural dixisse, but that/which vinci possit, it is, possit caveri.

lemmas.lexica: LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS naturalis; Blaise malum naturale=evil as a nature
LS concupiscentia=eager desire; Blaise Christian usage often sexual desire vs nuptiae
LS malum; Blaise malum naturale vs malum voluntatis
LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will

pass_b_english: If you admit desire’s evil cannot be conquered, you will profess yourself an advocate of shamefulness. But if you say you called this evil natural, yet capable of being conquered—that is, avoided—
People can avoid every sin when they can conquer the evil of desire. If lust is a natural evil and is conquered by love of virtue, all the more can the vices arising solely from the will be overcome.

choices.why: Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Contra Iulianum / Against Julian), including authorities Julian quoted; Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
